title: Large-scale NMR simulation on a trapped-ion quantum computer
authors: Pascal Stadler, Alec Owens, Etienne Granet, David Muñoz Ramo, Michael Marthaler
abstract: Simulating nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra is a promising application of quantum simulation. Using Quantinuum's System Model H2, a trapped-ion quantum computer, we demonstrate an end-to-end, large-scale digital NMR simulation of a classically challenging benchmark molecule, 1,2-di-tert-butyl-diphosphane. We implement a hardware-efficient reduction of the nuclear-spin Hamiltonian, enabling Trotterized real-time evolution of an effective 21-spin model with tailored error suppression to reduce the effects of device noise. The reconstructed liquid-state proton NMR spectrum agrees with classical reference calculations and reproduces key spectroscopic features that previous quantum hardware demonstrations did not capture. Given the widespread use of NMR in chemical analysis and industrial research, these results advance digital quantum simulation of NMR spectra towards practical quantum utility.
summary: This paper presents a large-scale, end-to-end quantum simulation of NMR spectra using a trapped-ion quantum computer. By employing significant Hamiltonian reduction and advanced error suppression, the authors successfully simulated a complex molecule, achieving spectral fidelity matching classical results. This work advances the practical utility of quantum computation for chemical analysis.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of simulating complex Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectra, which is a key application for quantum simulation, on near-term quantum hardware.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated an end-to-end, large-scale digital NMR simulation of a complex molecule, reproducing key spectral features that previous quantum hardware demonstrations could not achieve.
method: The simulation employs Trotterized real-time quantum evolution on a trapped-ion quantum computer, utilizing a hardware-efficient reduction of the full spin Hamiltonian to manage circuit depth.
model_or_system: The system is the 1,2-di-tert-butyl-diphosphane molecule, modeled as a 22-spin system. The simulation is performed on a trapped-ion quantum computer (Quantinuum H2), requiring significant Hamiltonian reduction to fit the available qubits and gate depth.
key_observables: The reconstructed liquid-state proton NMR spectrum, time-domain correlation functions ($C_{xx}(t), C_{yx}(t)$), and spectral fidelity compared to classical reference calculations.
important_parameters: The simulation involves an effective 21-spin model, uses Trotter steps up to 70 (or more in early stages), and is constrained by hardware gate depth and noise characteristics.
main_assumptions: The primary approximation involves projecting the full Hamiltonian onto a 21-dimensional subspace by rewriting the phosphorus subsystem in the singlet-triplet basis. Error suppression techniques are also crucial assumptions for fidelity.
figures_summary: Figures compare the simulated H2-1 hardware spectrum against classical reference spectra, showing agreement in key features like double-peak structures, and illustrate the impact of leakage and finite-shot noise.
paper_structure: The paper details the physical problem (NMR simulation), outlines the necessary Hamiltonian reduction (from 22 spins to 21 effective spins), describes the quantum simulation workflow (Trotterization, error mitigation), and concludes by validating the results against classical benchmarks on the trapped-ion hardware.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges quantum computation with molecular physics by applying quantum simulation techniques to a chemically relevant problem (NMR), showcasing the feasibility of quantum computation for complex, many-body quantum systems.
